claims.text: The HfNbTiVAl10 alloy exhibits a hierarchical heterostructure.
High-resolution microstructural characterization can capture spatial distributions of constituent phases and defects in HfNbTiVAl10.
A machine-learning regression model can be trained using a limited set of tensile and fracture-test data.
The hierarchical heterostructure mediates local stress and strain distributions.
The relevant local stress and strain effects can be encoded through characterized microstructural features for machine-learning prediction.
Multiscale features such as grain boundaries and phase distributions correlate with the alloy's tensile and fracture responses.
Data-driven regression can bypass computationally intensive steps used by established mechanical simulations.

Combining microstructural characterization with machine-learning regression will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior more accurately than conventional simulation methods.
The proposed model will reduce prediction computation time by at least 50% relative to established simulation methods.
The proposed model will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior within 10% of experimental measurements.
Finite-element and other continuum-based simulations are typically more time-consuming than the proposed machine-learning approach.
Predictive performance may fail when microstructural variability, inhomogeneities, or defects fall outside the training distribution.
Predictive performance may fail at strain rates or temperatures outside those used for model calibration.
Experimental data describing the precise multiscale mechanical behavior of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 are limited.
